Maladaptive Strategies.value: perform mental rituals to prevent bad things from happening again
Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank

Negative Appraisals.value: The event happened because of the way I acted
I should have protected others and I failed

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: For a trauma type of trauma to a loved one, the appraisal that the patient's own body has been permanently damaged is hard to reconcile unless the patient also directly sustained major physical injury, which is not reflected elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
issues.explanation: Avoidance of medical cues can fit some trauma-to-a-loved-one cases, but in this profile it appears to be driven by a personal bodily injury/medical trauma theme that is otherwise unsupported except by the implausible physical-vulnerability appraisal, making this item clinically incoherent with the rest of the profile.

vignette:
Sister Margaret had spent forty-two years in the convent, most of them teaching third grade at St. Catherine's, but nothing in her life had prepared her for the morning Sister Anne collapsed in the garden. It was late October, and they had been pruning the rose bushes together, Margaret holding the clippers while Anne reached for a tangled branch. The sound Anne made was not a cry but a soft exhale, and then she was on the ground, her face the color of old linen. Margaret knelt beside her, fumbling for a pulse, and in that moment she knew-knew with a certainty that felt like judgment-that she had done everything wrong. She had hesitated before calling for help, had wasted precious seconds trying to remember the number for the parish office instead of dialing 911 immediately. The ambulance came, but by the time they reached the hospital, Anne had suffered a massive stroke. She survived, but she would never speak again, never walk, never tend her roses. Margaret replayed those seconds endlessly, and each time she reached the same conclusion: the event happened because of the way she acted. She had failed to protect someone she loved, and that failure meant something fundamental about her-she could not rely on herself. These thoughts burrowed into her like splinters, and the more she tried to pull them out, the deeper they went.

The memory of that morning was both brutally clear and strangely fragmented. Some moments-the feel of Anne's wrist under her fingers, the exact shade of yellow on the fallen rose petals-were so vivid they felt like photographs she could hold. But other moments were entirely blank: she could not remember dialing the phone, could not remember what she said to the dispatcher, could not remember who drove her to the hospital. The gaps terrified her because they confirmed what she already believed: her mind was unreliable, just as her actions had been. And then there were the times the memory came without warning. A flash of yellow in a parishioner's garden, the scent of damp earth after rain, the sound of a woman's soft laugh-any of these could drop her back into that garden, her hands shaking, Anne's body still on the ground. Each time it happened, she felt the old certainty return: you failed, you failed, you failed.

Margaret began to avoid the garden entirely, taking a long route around the convent to the back door so she would not have to see the rose bushes. She stopped walking past the hospital on her errands, even if it meant adding twenty minutes to her trip. But the avoidance spread further. Anything that reminded her of Anne-a particular hymn, the smell of lavender soap, the sight of someone pruning-became a trigger she had to navigate. She began to perform small mental rituals, counting silently to seven whenever she passed a certain corner, repeating a prayer under her breath whenever an intrusive image surfaced, because she had come to believe that if she did not, something worse would happen. She knew, in the rational part of her mind, that these rituals made no sense, but the fear that followed each unbidden memory was so sharp that the rituals felt like the only thing standing between her and disaster. And each time she performed one, she saw more clearly how broken she was, how incapable of trusting herself, and this only deepened her conviction that she had failed Anne because of some flaw at her core.

The rituals and avoidance did not stop the memories; they seemed to sharpen them. The more she tried not to think about that morning, the more clearly she saw Anne's face, the more the blank spots in her memory felt like accusations. She found herself unable to concentrate during evening prayers, her mind snagging on the same loop of images and self-blame. Her community noticed her distance, but she could not explain it-what would she say? That she had killed Sister Anne through her own incompetence? That she could not be trusted with anything important anymore? The silence itself became another ritual, another way of trying to control a world that felt dangerous.

What finally brought her to seek help was a Sunday in February, when she was asked to lead the congregation in a prayer for the sick. She opened her mouth and could not speak. The words were there, but her throat closed, and all she could see was Anne's face on the hospital pillow. She fled the chapel, and later that evening, she called the diocesan counseling line. She was afraid-afraid that talking about it would make the memories worse, afraid that she would be judged as she judged herself-but she was more afraid of what she was becoming. She hoped, though she could barely admit it, that someone might show her a way out of the loop she had been running for months, that there might be a version of herself who could look at a rose bush and feel nothing but peace.
